The study outlines strengths and best practices for utilizing explanations to detect bias, while also noting three primary limitations: their difficulty in estimating the extent of bias, the potential for explanations to inject new bias, and the human effort required, which can sometimes prove inefficient.

This paper examines Hardy-Rellich inequalities associated with perturbed Laplacians, demonstrating that specific non-trivial angular modifications to the free operator typically enhance the inequality and, at times, yield an estimate unattainable in the original case. Prominent examples involve magnetic field induction, which reflects the diamagnetic phenomenon previously established by Laptev and Weidl \cite{LW1999} for Hardy inequalities and subsequently by Evans and Lewis \cite{EL2005} for Rellich inequalities. Despite this, our research suggests to the current understanding that such magnetic effects in the context of Hardy-Rellich inequalities represent a novel area. After deriving the optimal form of these inequalities, it is proven that no function within the relevant domain serves as the maximizer for the best constant.

Alan Turing introduced the Turing test in 1950, establishing as a core mission for AI the capacity for computing systems to emulate human action. Yet, computer applications most profoundly expand intelligence precisely where their strengths diverge from inherent human capabilities. A more effective objective transcending the replication of humanity focuses on augmentation instead. Consequently, this article reviews various systems advancing both individual human intellect and social intelligence through such differentiation rather than imitation.

Mechanistic cardiac electrophysiology models enable personalized simulations of the heart's electrical patterns and resultant surface ECGs. Consequently, these synthetic signals contain well-defined ground truth labels of the underlying diseases, serving as a resource to benchmark machine learning tools designed for ECG analysis alongside authentic patient data. Recent applications of synthetic ECGs include augmenting sparse clinical datasets or acting as stand-ins specifically to boost the performance of AI on real-world test data. To this end, we constructed an new synthetic repository of 16,900 12-lead ECGs generated through electrophysiological modeling; this collection is evenly distributed between healthy controls and seven distinct disease categories, which further include six sub-types for myocardial infarction. A feature-based comparison of the virtual population against a publicly accessible clinical dataset indicates that the synthetic tracels faithfully depict both healthy and various pathological subgroups. This database is partitioned into training, validation, and testing subsets to facilitate the advancement and unbiased evaluation of new machine learning methodologies.

Recent breakthroughs have introduced powerful generative models capable of creating high-quality images and videos based on specific text prompts. Despite this success, existing methods struggle when tasked with the complexities of story visualization. Such narratives require navigating ambiguous references, resolving co-reference, and dynamically deciding where to maintain consistency in characters and settings based on plot progression. To tackle these difficulties, this paper introduces a new autoregressive framework utilizing diffusion, equipped with a visual memory module designed to automatically track character and background context across generated frames. Within this system, sentence-soft attention over these memories facilitates precise resolution of visual references, enabling the model to selectively preserve scene and actor consistency as needed. We enhance the MUGEN dataset by incorporating additional roles and recurring scenes into multi-sentence storylines, then conduct experiments on both MUGEN and FlintstonesSV. The results demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art models in producing visually high-quality story frames and successfully models accurate correspondence between protagonists and their environments.

We introduce Magic Layouts, a technique for parsing screenshots or hand-drawn sketches of user interfaces. Our primary advancement lies in extending current detection tools to leverage a learned structural prior specific to UI designs, thereby enabling the robust identification of components such as buttons and text fields. Specifically, this research establishes a prior over mobile UI patterns to capture common spatial associations between various UI elements. Utilizing this prior to condition region proposals improves performance in parsing layouts for hand-drawn interfaces and app screenshots, a capability demonstrated through an interactive application designed for swiftly creating UX digital prototypes.

Advances in representation learning coupled with the vast availability of high-quality medical imaging data have driven a swift surge in the application of machine learning to 3D medical image analysis. Specifically, 3D convolution neural networks have become indispensable tools within medical imaging, aiding professionals in disease diagnostics by leveraging patient care expertise. Nonetheless, the computational demands of training deep architectures, such as deep convolution neural networks, on high-resolutions three-dimensional volumes of Computed Tomography scans, complicate their use. There is thus an urgent need to develop robust learning approaches that focus directly on two dimensional slicing rather than entire 3D scans, yet still enable deep learning methodologies. Recently introduced into medical imaging research is the practice of extracting descriptors using pre defined slice level classifiers based upon adjacent scans of images that show CT findings which lead new lines into 3D resolution levels when applied with CT scans having per slice labels including the RSনা ICH Challenge data. The model predicts presence of intracranial hemorrhage while classifying them again into 5 major sub-types; creating a 3D resolution level capable of generating single slice level predictions that outperformance baseline models by obtaining top results within 4% in the competition. Experimental data also demonstrates this approach's potential in dealing with MRI and other three-dimensional medical imaging techniques. Thus, authors will publish codes freely available at paper submission.

This investigation examines stabilization strategies for nonlinear difference equation systems utilizing modified Target-Oriented Control to achieve selected equilibrium points, across both deterministic and stochastic contexts. We analyze how stochastic variations in the control parameters impact the dynamics and further validate our theoretical results by applying a numerical example to the H\'{e}non and Lozi maps.

We have created a simulation-driven approach for spectrally analyzing X-ray CCD data corrupted by pile-up, ensuring zero loss in photon statistics. Since pile-up instills complex nonlinear detector responses, our method utilizes sophisticated simulations to model critical stages of an X-ray observation, spanning physical interactions, signal processing, readout, and data reduction. These simulations authentically replicate both background and mimic X-ray-like events arising from photon accumulation within individual or groups of neighboring pixels, thereby establishing a nonlinear spectral framework capable of addressing affected datasets. To validate this approach, we applied the framework—tuned with optimized detector parameters—to Suzaku XIS observations across scenarios with minimal, moderate, and significant pile-up (specifically PKS ~ 2155-304, Aquilae X-1, and the Crab Nebula, respectively). While the méthode yields outcomes consistent with traditional linear analysis under conditions of negligible pile-up, it effectively corrects recognized pile-up artifacts like spectral hardening and reduced flux for more affected cases. These findings align with results from the core-exclusion technique or observations with superior temporal resolutions that avoid pile-up. By optimizing simulation parameters appropriately, this framework extends to all types of X-ray astronomical CCDs and is prepared to support future missions like XRISM.

The discrepancy in the Hubble-Lemaitre tension represents one of the most critical challenges in modern cosmology. Previous efforts have primarily concentrated on harmonizing the Hubble constant values derived from high-precision cosmic microwave background data versus those measured by the local distance ladder. However, priorit solely on this single metric, $\H_0$ obscures the root of the conflict, which actually stems from inconsistent distance measurements. For theoretical models to effectively address this, they must precisely account for the observed distances rather than just aiming to reproduce a predefined $\H_0$ value. Our findings demonstrate, using the novel MonteJava-integrated suite `distanceladder', that neglecting distances in favor of $\H_0$ can erroneously prompt cosmologists to detect new physics in models altering late-time evolution. Consequently, we advise the observational community to publicly distribute raw distance datasets to model developers instead of offering only the resulting Hubble constants.

This report outlines how the University of Copenhagen and Aalborg University took part in the 2020 TREC-COVID Challenge, an international search engine contest hosted by the NIST and its Text Retrieval Conference division. The objective of the event was to determine the most effective strategies for accurately extracting detailed medical science regarding COVID-19 from CORD-19, then's largest compilation of vetted COVID-19 research. Established following a March 2020 joint White House mobilization and later shared on Kaggle by the Allen Institute for AI, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, several universities, and others, CORD-19 comprised over 200,000 peer-reviewed papers (more than half with full text) covering COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, and linked viral issues. Participants were tasked with two primary goals: (1) retrieving factual, precise scientific answers in response to queries crafted by medical professionals, and (2) ordering those results based on their relevance to the input. This paper details our engagement in the TREC-COVID competition framework along with our analysis on the strengths and challenges of top-tier technology when addressing the urgent need for specialized scientific retrieval within an expanding body of texts during global lockdowns and pandemics.

Over the past twenty years, Distance Metric Learning (DML) has garnered significant interest due to its effectiveness in quantifying similarity between individuals using correctly labeled pairwise data provided by domain experts. However, such precise and labeled pairwise information is frequently vulnerable in real-world applications, such as when assessing patient similarity. This study uniquely investigates the potential for attackers to infer individual relationships through leaked pairwise data during distance metric learning, while introducing differential pairwise privacy (DPP)—a generalization of standard differential privacy tailored for metric learning safety. Unlike traditional differential privacy, which assumes independent samples and thus fails to address the interdependencies of pairwise data, DPP resolves this issue by reframing the worst-case scenario to fully exploit correlations within the underlying undirected graph of the pairs. Furthermore, the work formally defines the requirements for differentially private distance metric learning algorithms on this structured data. By way of validation, the authors provide a case study on an algorithm using contrastive loss to illustrate the implementation specifics of DPP-DML. Notably, they propose a sensitivity reduction technique to maintain the utility of the resulting distance metrics. Experimental results across both artificial toy datasets and standard benchmarks confirm that the proposed framework effectively protects pairwise data privacy while sustaining high utility; specifically, even at a strict privacy budget, the accuracy impact remains negligible, declining by less than 1% on every evaluated dataset.

Random states and quantum operations hold significant both practical and foundational importance. This study explores the entanglement characteristics of random hypergraph states, which extend graph state concepts by utilizing generalized controlled-phase gates acting on a standard initial product state. We specifically analyze two ensembles created through random Controlled-Z (CZ) and Controlled-Controlled-Z (CCZ) gates. Leveraging combinational counting and tensor network formalisms, we analytically demonstrate that both the entanglement entropy and average subsystem purity obey the same volume law across these two ensembles. However, they differ markedly regarding typicality; while purification in the CCZ ensemble exhibits large purity fluctuations and lacks universal behavior, the CZ ensemble shows large fluctuations universally. We examine the broader consequences of these findings concerning quantum chaos and the development of entanglement complexity.

We introduce a novel one-shot domain adaptation approach that takes an input of a trained StyleGAN generator producing domain A images and just a single reference image from domain B. This algorithm translates any GAN output from domain A into domain B. Compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques, our method offers two primary advantages. Firstly, it delivers superior visual quality, significantly reducing overfitting. Secondly, it enables greater flexibility in controlling the domain gap, allowing users to select specific aspects of the reference image that define domain B. To achieve this, our technical strategy leverages a pre-trained StyleGAN as well as pre-trained CLIP for domain gap representation. To shift the generator from outputting domain A images to domain B images while preventing excessive adherence to single-image attributes, the authors introduce novel regularizers designed to optimize the generator weights. Experimental findings demonstrate substantial visual enhancements over previous solutions alongside various applications that underscore enhanced control capabilities.

This study addresses the challenge of learning control policies for stochastic systems that ensure stabilization within a defined set using standard $1$ probability. Our methodology introduces the innovation of "stabilizing randomization supermartingales" (sRSMs), a concept designed specifically for this purpose. By using these tools we are overcoming the drawbacks inherent in prior methods by allowing the system to exit a stable state, which is a constraint in preexisting literature which doesn't allow for leaving this safe zone once it is achieved. We propose training neural networks to autonomously discover control policies along with the sRSMs themselves, which effectively confirm the stability of system with $ $ probability; experiments prove that our learning approach effectively yields policies that are proven stabilizers, both theoretically and empirically.

This study explores how stochastic, randomly oriented cellular traction forces drive fluidization within a vertex-based model of epithelial layers. We determine that this fluidization triggers at a specific threshold value of the traction force magnitude. Our findings introduce a mechanism where active force generation induces fluidization, a process potentially significant for the dynamics of biological tissues.

This work examines the relationship between sequential system ID and control for linear time-invariant systems, covering both indirect control via data-driven methods and contemporary direct data-driven control. The latter approach determines optimal decisions compatible with recorded data organized in a Hankel matrix, enhanced via appropriate regularization. We cast these distinct challenges in terms of behavioral systems theory and parametric optimization, then connect them using a multi-objective framework to balance system ID and control goals. Illustrative methods, including subspace predictive control and low-rank approximation from subspace techniques, enforce trajectory consistency by restricting them to a Hankel-based non-parametric predictor or its column space respectively. In these cases, direct data-driven control regularized by suitable penalties emerges as a convex relaxation of the indirect method, with regularization implicitly performing system ID. Our analysis also identifies a new regularization term and provides a credible hypothesis for the outstanding empirical performance of direct methods when applied to nonlinear systems.

Widely spreading uncertainties have rendered the interaction between wind power and the electricity grid more complex, complicating modeling and resolution attempts. To address the unit commitment (UC) problem, this study proposes a method that accounts for inherent multifaceted uncertainties in wind power and the grid by utilizing probabilistic, possibilistic, and interval measures. Evidence theory (ET) is leveraged to comprehensively manage these uncertainties and integrate uncertain variables into a Dempster-Shafer structure. The methodology introduces power losses into power balance equations, using extended affine arithmetic (EAA) to estimate the uncertainty arising from the propagation of losses caused by the aforementioned variances. To handle the mixed-discrete non-linear characteristics of the developed optimization framework, a tailored enhanced Grey Wolf Optimizer (E-GWO) algorithm is deployed, specifically utilizing Binary GWO (BGWO) for generating commitment schedules, the GWO technique for economic dispatch (ED), and the enhanced E-GWO as an overarching solver. The validity and scalability of this proposed model and methodology were validated through case studies conducted on both the IEEE 30-node test and a practical Chinese power system comprising 183 bus terminals.

As social media platforms shift from text-centric spaces to multi-modal environments featuring images and videos, misinformation tactics are adapting accordingly. Capitalizing on the fact that visual media appeals to existing attention cycles while text is often overlooked hastily, distributors increasingly exploit inconsistencies between different modalities, such as misaligned text/images, rather than just misleading individual elements. Consequently, significant research has developed automatic detection tools targeting these cross-modal discordancess across the web. Our method employs a unique optimization-driven approach to crafting queries used for this probed extraction. Contrariwise to traditional model inversion techniques, this fingerprinting strategy avoids dependency on fine-grained outputs, structural specifications, or training datasets used during creation. Purpose: We aimed to investigate ways in which platform-providing public entities can resolve specific challenges by fostering collaboration within their Open Government Data (OGD) networks, encompassing published data alongside related Open Source Software (OSS) and standards. Methodology: An exploratory multi-case study examining four distinct OGD ecosystems was performed; data were gathered using semi-structured interviews and long-term engagement within one instance, coded with pre-existing thematic sets. Results: Each case was described through this coding framework and synthesized into a conceptual model outlining key OGD ecosystem attributes. The findings illustrate various collaboration mechanisms influenced by platform ownership types, varying ecosystem scopes, potential provider roles, processes for facilitating open collaboration, and approaches to data sharing, OSS development, and standard setting. This paper introduces a new control design method for nonlinear systems that utilizes model-free policy optimization to learn a linearizing controller for a physical system with uncertain dynamics. Feedback linearization renders a nonlinear plant's input-output behavior linear through a specific feedback controller, allowing desired trajectories to be tracked with established linear control techniques; however, traditional approaches depend on knowing the system's precise model and having easily identifiable, simple parameters. Conversely, our proposed model-free method approximates this linearizing controller by leveraging general function approximation architectures. By defining a continuous-time optimization problem over the learned controller parameters—where optimal solutions yield the best linearizing results—we establish conditions ensuring strong convexity in this probability learning task, thereby mathematically guaranteeing the recovery of the true controller for the physical plant. Subsequently, we demonstrate how policy optimization algorithms address discrete-time approximations using empirical data from real devices. The proposed framework's effectiveness is validated through both simulation results and implementation on an actual robotic platform.

Large-scale epidemiographic research typically features a frequent, cost-effective, non-invasive assessment of disease state, interspersed with less frequent administrations of the gold-standard test. Conversely, limiting analysis to the infrequently collected, accurate gold-standard data often yields low statistical efficiency. Consequently, researchers have formulated an augmented likelihood function that jointly integrates data from these fallible outcomes and the primary gold-standard assessments. Through simulation studies, they demonstrate that this new approach significantly boosts statistical efficiency compared to standard strategies for handling interval-censored survival data that neglect auxiliary information. Furthermore, they adapted the model for complex survey designs to facilitate its application within a motivating case study. Specifically, the researchers applied the new joint modeling framework to data from the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos to examine how energy and protein consumption influence diabetes incidence rates. Additionally, they successfully combined the primary methodology with regression calibration to handle covari measurement error inherent in reported dietary habits.

A word-to-word function is considered rational whenever a non-deterministic one-way transducer realizes it. For finite words, classical theory establishes that any such rational function is regular—effectively computable by either a deterministic two-way transducer or, alternatively, a deterministic streaming string transducer (which uses registers on a one-way automaton). However, this equivalence breaks down over infinite words because a non-deterministic one-way transducer possesses the capacity to guess and verify run properties, such as patterns occurring infinitely frequently, attributes beyond the reach of deterministic machines. In this work, we delineate the subset of rational infinite-word functions also computable by a deterministic two-way transducer; this class corresponds precisely to the rational continuous functions and offers a decidable method for identifying it, thereby resolving a longstanding inquiry raised by Dave and his colleagues in prior research.

Despite notable advancements in 3D face reconstruction, existing methods that rely on orthogonal projections often fail to produce accurate and consistent results at very short viewing distances due to perspective-induced distortions. This paper proposes a solution that jointly reconstructs 3D face meshes within the world coordinate frame while simultaneously predicting 2D face landmarks to overcome limitations of perspective-based projection techniques. By combining predicted vertices and 2D landmarks with the Perspective-n-Pose (PnP) solver, we estimate the 6-DoF face pose to effectively capture perspective representation. This method secured the first-ranking position on the ECCV 2022 WCPA challenge and demonstrates visual robustness across varying identities, expressions, and poses, with all training models and code made publicly available to support ongoing research.

Using combined first principles energy calculations and an innovative "modified basin-hopping" technique, this study examines the electronic and atomic configurations of the (001)-Si/(001)-$\gamma$-Al2O3 interface. Research reveals that in the newly proposed abrupt model interface, oxygen creates Si-O bonds alongside novel unexpected covalent Si-Al bonds that result in four-fold coordination for every interface silicon atom. Furthermore, the interface demonstrates ideal electronic characteristics, exhibiting an expansive LDA band gap and absent gap-level states when unpassivated. These findings suggest that uncontaminated interfaces between semiconductors and oxides can effectively be achieved.

Recent research on the question answering (QA) field has focused on the multi-hop reasoning framework applied to Knowledge Graphs (KG), as it facilitates efficient and explainable reasoning. However, due to their strictly linear reasoning mechanism, multi-hop methods fail to effectively handle n-ary fact questions. To address this gap, the author identifies two critical enhancements: first, evolving the fundamental reasoning unit from entity or relation to "fact"; second, shifting the reasoning architecture from a chain-based to a tree-based structure. Consequently, this work introduces a new fact-tree reasoning framework that converts questions into fact trees and executes iterative reasoning across them to derive the correct answer. A thorough evaluation conducted on a new n-ary fact KGQA dataset, created in this study, reveals the proposed framework's ability to effectively boost answer prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the model was tested on two existing binary KGQA datasets, demonstrating that it retains a potent reasoning capability compared to various leading state-of-the-art baselines. Overall, this contribution not only offers a preliminary baseline but also holds direct significance for tackling future complex reasoning challenges.

This study introduces a fluid model composed of polydisperse rounded hard rectangles, where rectangular core dimensions remain constant but roundness is defined by a convex envelope of a disk sliding along the core's perimeter. Our findings show that increasing roundness significantly diminishes the teteratic phase's regions of stability, while greatly weakening and restricting the interval of first-order transitions for the teteratic-nematic and isotropic-nematic phases. Strong fractionation occurs due to polydispersity between coexisting phases, leading to a nematic enrichment in lower-roundness particles, and sufficient levels of polydispersity alongside specific aspect ratios convert an originally second-order one-component fluid transition from isotropic to nematic into a first-order one. Notably, we also observed a "packing-fraction-inversion" effect at high polydispersity thresholds where the coexisting isotropic phase exhibits a greater packing fraction than its liquid-crystal equivalent (nematic).

This study examines the connection between monetary poverty and production economic activity by integrating network science, graph theory, and regression techniques with the relatedness framework of the product space. Two distinct product-level indicators, reflecting poverty patterns on short and long timescales respectively, are constructed using the network topology, allowing the authors to assess how a country's productive capacity shapes its present and prospective poverty trajectories. Even at absolute zero, extremely flexible elastic layers demonstrate nonlinear elasticity primarily through bending mechanisms, with an increasingly complex behavior observed at finite temperatures. In this study, molecular dynamics simulations investigate the vibrations of a thermally varying two-dimensional elastic sheet that remains anchored at one end to its zero-temperature length. We identify a distinct "tilt phase," where the sheet fluctuates around a non-vertical average plane relative to the horizontal, effectively breaking reflectional symmetry. By examining how the phase behavior varies with sheet aspect ratio and temperature, we demonstrate that this tilt constitutes a transverse buckling instability triggered by thermal fluctuations combined with clamping conditions. We construct an analytical framework to predict the boundaries between inclined and non-inclined regions of the phase diagram, which shows qualitative alignment with our simulation data. This phenomenon highlights unique responses emerging from the manipulation of inherent geometric factors, such as aspect ratios, rather than external field inputs, creating an especially fertile domain for investigating 2D mechanical metamaterials.

Most standard models describing jet quenching rely heavily on the approximation of straight eikonal trajectories for jet propagation; while this holds well for very hard jets, it becomes less accurate for jets with moderate or low momentum. In this study, I have extended these 2-to-3 processes by relaxing part of that eikonal approximation and discovered that non-eikonal effects induce a $(15–20)\%$ depletion in the differential cross-section for moderately hard jets. Specifically, in the centre-of-momentum frame, $qq' \to qq'g$ scattering at angles beyond the $\pm 0.52\pi$ limit is strictly nonexistent in contrast to $gg \to ggg$, which permits a scattering range up to $\pi$. This dynamic holds potential significant impacts regarding the suppression observed in hadronic energy distributions at low transverse momenta.

The precise function of quantization in implicit and coordinate-based neural architectures remains unclear. Our analysis indicates that applying a standard fixed-precision quantization strategy during training yields suboptimal results in low-bit regimes because of how neural weights distributions evolve over time. This study demonstrates, however, that adopting a non-uniform, cluster-based quantization scheme substantially enhances weight encoding. We also characterize the trade-off between quantization levels and network expressiveness, proofning that it becomes feasible—albeit at the cost of higher memory requirements—to restore data using purely binary neural networks. Our experimental validation, conducted on both 2D image restoration and 3D radiance fields using NeuRadFields, confirms our propositions: incorporating these quantization techniques alongside architectural search enables the model to achieve compression surpassing an eighteen-kilobound limit, reducing the representation of NeRF models to 335 times smaller with minimal accuracy loss.

We investigate the dynamical behavior of a complex scalar field within a broken-symmetry regime under an oscillating spacetime metric. Using (2+1)-dimensional computer simulations, we demonstrate how oscillations in geometry can trigger excitations that evolve to create topological vortices, ultimately settling the field into a disordered state. Analysis of momentum and frequency spectra indicates that parametric resonance is responsible for these field disturbances. Notably, in a high-frequency limit where spacetime oscillation scales far exceed the field's mass, vortices cease to possess true topological character. However, under specific parameter configurations in this regime, a stable lattice comprising vortex-antivortex pairs can emerge sustainably. Additionally, we outline potential applications, such as understanding interior superfluid dynamics within neutron stars during binary mergers and the generation of excitations near astrophysical strong gravitational wave sources in the context of ultralight axion-like fields.

We present a resource-efficient time-scaling method designed to improve quantum protocols within non-Hermitian environments. This technique requires no additional couplings and significantly boosts quantum fidelity using similar resources. We analyze its application to state transfer in open, two- and three-level systems and derive the quantum speed limit for non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. Notably, with tailored driving fields, this scaling approach maintains optimal speed relative to the derived quantum speed limit while substantially reducing state norm damping.

Animals have developed intricate visual mechanisms to interpret movement within complicated settings, aiding their perception accordingly. Our key contributions include the introduction of a streamlined Transformer variant designed for splitting optical flow images against primary objects and backgrounds; self-supervised architecture training that eliminates the need for hand-labeled data; an in-depth analysis of essential methodological components coupled with extensive ablation experiments; and an evaluation across public benchmarks (DAVIS2016, DAVIS, FBMS54). Even though our approach relies exclusively on optical flow, it yields superior performance or results on par with leading un supervised methods while executing approximately an order of magnitude faster. Furthermore, testing on a rigorous camouflage kit (MCRA) demonstrated our performance significantly surpasses most un supervised prior methods while holding its own better against the top supervised technique. These findings emphasize the vital role of motion cues as well as reveal a potential preference in typical video segmentation systems for over visual appearances rather than movement.
